examples: The next morning a fine, steady drizzle was falling, and the garden smelt cleansed and fresh.
On his way to the workshop, Tom stopped to have a root around under the washing line.
Tom stopped to have a root around under the washing line, but he didn't find Aunt Emily's ring.
A blackbird hopped about on the lawn, scattering flecks of water with its feet as it hunted for worms.
A blackbird hopped about on the lawn, scattering flecks of water with its feet.
The robotic lawnmower was idle at its charging point, obediently avoiding the wet.
In the workshop he fell on to the battered office chair opposite his cockpit.
He fell on to the battered office chair, letting his walking stick clatter to the floor.
The old boatshed was full of a partially organized clutter, as if Uncle Ted had just stepped outside.
Arranged along one wall were soldering irons and electrical testing equipment.
On another wall was a bandsaw and a metal working lathe.
Scattered around the floor were spools of wires, oil drums and pumps.
Scattered around were outboard motors with their insides showing.
The motors lay with their insides showing, like anaesthetized patients in the middle of half-finished operations.
Next to the cockpit was an old trestle table which served as a desk.
On the desk there was a wonky Airfix model of a Hawk T1.
A wonky Airfix model of a Hawk T1 in Red Arrows livery sat on the desk.
There was a photograph of Tom's father, smiling on the tarmac by the nose cone of his Tornado.
A photograph showed Tom's father smiling by the nose cone of his Tornado.
The sky behind the plane was still blue and bright and big, somehow full of promise.
He ran through the preflight checks.
A skylight opened and folded itself back against the pitched slate roof with a hiss.
He twisted a knob and a sound like a nest of angry wasps could be heard in the rafters.
A sound like a nest of angry wasps could be heard in the rafters.
A CCTV image showed the lawn, surrounded by the red-barked cedar trees.
A sleek black machine emerged from the cavity of the roof like a butterfly from a chrysalis.
The machine emerged from the roof like a butterfly from a chrysalis.
A sleek black machine about the size of a raven rose from the roof.
Tom felt his world expand, and the worries of the week recede.
He accelerated towards the river, skimming the top of the cedars.
He left behind only the indignant squawk of a magpie to disturb the silence.
Only the indignant squawk of a magpie remained to disturb the silence.
Strangely, in that infinity of sky, it was the little things Tom noticed most.
An early-morning swimmer plunged from a jetty into the water.
He noticed the tottering steps of a newborn fawn hidden in a bramble thicket.
The tottering steps of a newborn fawn were hidden in a bramble thicket.
A newborn fawn lay hidden in a bramble thicket.
He noticed the first scratch of a plough in a field.
Tom could see specks of dew on the fox's whiskers before it sauntered on its way.
The fox sauntered on its way, tail swaying in the crisp morning light.
Once he had tried to round up a flock of sheep, herding them into the corner of a field.
He had tagged on to the end of a formation of migrating geese.
He followed a formation of migrating geese all the way to Morecambe Bay.
He followed the geese while the sun rose in a tiger-striped sky.
His love of flying had begun when his father had hoisted him into his cockpit on his ninth birthday.
It was like the zingy straight-from-the-factory smell that hits you when you unpackage a new gadget.
The smell hits you when you unpackage a new electronic gadget for the first time.
The zingy smell hits you when you unpackage a new electronic gadget.
It was that cockpit smell, almost a taste, gulped down in a few excited breaths.
His dad talked him round the baffling array of dials and switches.
His dad talked him round the baffling array of dials and switches.
It was the sight of the man with the ponytail that shook him out of these thoughts.
It was his hair, shiny in the wet, that gave him away.
Rigg Knott was an even-sided hill surrounded by conifers.
It was towards the peak, with its limestone crags rising through the bracken, that the woman was gazing.
Limestone crags rose through the bracken on the side of the hill.
It was towards this peak that the woman was gazing.
He had plenty of flight time left to head to the third peak and see if his hunch was right.
He had plenty of flight time left to see if his hunch was right.
Passing over the campsite he could see families doggedly unpacking tents in the drizzle.
Normally she would be laden with pointing and waving tourists.
Apart from a lone crew member, her decks were deserted.
A lone crew member was coiling a rope at the bow.
His right leg had gone to sleep and was now wracked with cramp.
He stared at the screen, trying to piece together what he was looking at.
Each of them looked perfectly ordinary, blending into the landscape like everyone else.
But from the air their connection was unmistakable.
Tom moved nearer, mesmerized by the way she was absorbed in the game.
The girl, oblivious to the man at the trig point, stepped back into him.
She stepped back into the man and caused him to stumble.
For a moment his laptop was exposed, and Tom had a full view of the screen.
Tom felt a cold shiver work its way down his spine as he stared at the image.
There was something unsettling about these alien words.
The words appeared in matter-of-fact white on black computer font.
He dropped away from the hilltop like a stone.
Near the bottom he missed a drystone wall by inches and pulled up again.
He weaved through the graveyard and climbed to thirty feet behind the church.
He could glimpse the hill again through the slatted openings of the bell tower.
He could glimpse the top of the hill again through the slatted openings.
'Idiot!' Tom berated himself. 'He's looking for me now.'
He was setting a bearing for home when something airborne loomed past.
Something airborne loomed past, eclipsing the light for a second.
Something airborne loomed past, eclipsing the light for a second.
With a twist of the controls Tom spiralled skywards.
The sight of the helicopter filling the screen made his stomach churn.
It was a hefty military type with menacing air intakes.
The helicopter had menacing air intakes and a bulbous nose.
It was a hefty military type with menacing air intakes and a bulbous nose.
He could see Skylark's reflection in the pilot's helmet visor.
He felt the slap of turbulence as the aircraft pitched towards him.
He felt the slap of turbulence as the aircraft pitched towards him.
The drone was bounced and buffeted on a cushion of air.
Any faster and Skylark's wings would come off, or the motors would burn out.
His only chance to outmanoeuvre the helicopter was to flip up into a tight loop.
He hoped to flip over into a tight loop, ending up in its blind spot.
He planned to take refuge somewhere low before he could be found again.
A grey-haired man was attending to one of the rods fixed on either side of the boat.
When he could read the name of the boat, Tom exhaled with relief.
He pulled back, bracing himself for the sudden glare of sky.
He braced for the inverted horizon of the loop, but nothing happened.
He wiggled the stick sharply, but Skylark kept flying towards the shore.
He knew the drone's control signals had been jammed.
Jim looked up, pipe in his mouth, cradling a fish in both hands.
As the drone passed over the jagged shoreline into Dowthwaite Bay, the helicopter overtook it.
The helicopter overtook it, its rotors whipping up a circle of white.
A black police RIB had an armed crewman standing guard.
The Teal, tethered to the jetty, her hulk filling the inlet.
The Teal lay tethered to the jetty, her hulk filling the inlet.
The great ship sat in the narrow bay as out of place as a swan in a bathtub.
